Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Latin word

juxtā

adverb, and preposition with the accusative

close by, right next to; next to, beside, close by

In this lexicon

  • near

    also used · classical · Caes. B.G. 2.26.1: legiō, quae juxtā cōnstiterat (Lewis & Short)

  • next to

    the recommended word · classical · Caes. BC 1.16.4: juxtā mūrum castra posuit (Lewis & Short); Sall. Jug. 65.2: ut sellam juxtā pōneret

Notes

  1. 1juxtā: u left unmarked (the earlier draft of this record, jūxtā). Lewis & Short marks only the final ā, and the lexicon’s other records and the Latinitas loci write juxtā. De Vaan 318, s.v. juxta, derives it from Proto-Italic *jougVsto-, which would give a long u, but does not discuss the vowel. Left unmarked until it is settled.

Examples

  • hīc propter hunc adsiste: em, sīc volō.

    Stand here, next to him. There, that’s how I want it.Ter. Ad. 170

    In the entry for next to

  • tum in prātulō propter Platōnis statuam cōnsēdimus

    then we sat down on a little lawn beside the statue of PlatoCic. Brut. 24

    In the entry for next to

  • ībat rēx obsitus aevō et comitem Aenēān juxtā nātumque tenēbat ingrediēns variōque viam sermōne levābat

    the king, weighed down with years, walked on, keeping Aeneas and his son beside him, and lightened the way with talkVerg. A. 8.307–309

    In the entry for next to

  • mōre rēgum ut sellam juxtā pōneret

    (he asked) to set his chair beside him, as kings doSall. Jug. 65.2

    In the entry for next to

  • cētera intēctī tōtōs diēs juxtā focum atque ignem agunt

    otherwise unclothed, they spend whole days by the hearth and the fireTac. Germ. 17.1
